To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a population of the non‐migratory estuary fish Fundulus heterclitus (mummichogs) indigenous to a PCB‐contaminated superfund site (New Bedford harbor, MA, USA), demonstrated an inherited tolerance of local, dioxine‐like contaminants, suggesting that dioxin‐like contaminants have acted as selective agent, allowing the survival only of the most tolerant individuals and forming a dioxin‐tolerant population; 2) the
populations of the estuary fish Fundulus hetero­clitus that are adapted to dioxin‐like compounds reside where local conditions of dioxin‐ like compounds are toxic to sensitive fish.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the ecological and evolutionary consequences of exposure to environmental contaminants and the role of contaminants in shaping populations.
the effects of environmental contaminants on the evolution of populations of the esturaine fish Fundulus heteroclitus.
understanding and predicting the occurrence of genetic adaptations to environmental toxicants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study demonstrates the potential of a predictive model for the evolution of genetic tolerance to toxicants in natural populations of fish.
the occurrence of genetic adaptations in populations of the mummichog, Fundulus heterociltus, to dioxin-like contaminants in the environment was predicted and confirmed.

this study provides evidence that genetic adaptation to dixo‐like compounds has occurred in populations of the mummichog, Fundulus heterociltus, in response to exposure to dioxin-like compounds in the New Bedford Harbor, Massachusetts, USA, Superfund site, and that this genetic adaptation can be predicted based on laboratory studies with early life stages.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown a clear association between the presence of genetic adaptation to PCBs in a population of mummichog and the presence of PCB contamination at a site.
the evolution of tolerance to DLCs has occurred in F. heteroclitus populations at multiple sites along the east coast of the United States, and that the occurrence of this phenomenon is predictable.

the occurrence of genetic adaptations to DLCs in populations of F. heteroclitus is predicted by responses of early life stages to DLCs, and that the geographic scale of these effects is larger than previously envisioned.
The main takeaway from our work is that
populations can adapt to environmental contaminants, and that these adaptations can occur over a relatively short time period.
the occurrence of genetic adaptations to dioxin-like chemicals can be predicted from the responses of sensitive early-life stages to laboratory exposures to dioxin like chemicals.
the effects of contaminants on natural populations can be predicted based on the responses of sensitive early stages to laboratory exposures.
